papers.title: Dual-contrastive learning for spatial domain identification in spatial transcriptomics with STAMGC.
papers.summary: This paper introduces STAMGC, a computational method that uses dual-contrastive learning to identify spatial domains in spatial transcriptomics data. The approach likely combines graph-based modeling with contrastive learning techniques to better distinguish distinct tissue regions based on gene expression patterns and spatial location. This type of tool could improve the accuracy and resolution of mapping molecularly distinct areas within complex tissues like the brain.
papers.why: Since the abstract provides minimal detail, this appears to be a methods paper that could offer improved computational tools for spatial domain identification potentially useful for analyzing spatial transcriptomics data in brain regions containing interneurons and perineuronal nets.

papers.title: Spatial control of mitochondrial ubiquitination by the AMBRA1-RMC1-HUWE1 axis.
papers.summary: This paper investigates how the protein complex AMBRA1-RMC1-HUWE1 controls the tagging of damaged mitochondria with ubiquitin, a key step that marks them for removal. The study reveals how this tagging process is spatially organized within cells, showing that the location of ubiquitination matters for how mitochondria are selected for degradation. This adds mechanistic detail to our understanding of mitophagy, the cellular process that clears out faulty mitochondria.
papers.why: Understanding the molecular machinery that spatially regulates mitochondrial ubiquitination is directly relevant to studying mitophagy in neurons, since this pathway likely governs how neurons manage mitochondrial quality control in different subcellular compartments.

papers.title: SIRT1 in Neurodegenerative Diseases: Molecular Mechanisms, Disease Relevance, and Therapeutic Potential.
papers.summary: This paper is a review of SIRT1, a NAD+-dependent deacetylase, and its roles in neurodegenerative diseases. It covers the molecular mechanisms by which SIRT1 influences processes like protein aggregation, oxidative stress, and mitochondrial function in the brain. The review also discusses SIRT1's relevance across various neurodegenerative conditions and its potential as a therapeutic target.
papers.why: SIRT1 is a key regulator of mitophagy and autophagy pathways in neurons, directly relevant to the mechanistic focus of this PhD project on neuronal quality control in the brain.

papers.title: Advances in Calcium Transients and Autophagy.
papers.summary: This paper appears to review recent findings on how calcium transients—brief fluctuations in intracellular calcium concentration—regulate autophagy, the cellular process for degrading and recycling damaged components. Calcium signaling is known to influence key autophagy regulators such as AMPK, CaMKK2, and mTOR pathways. The abstract provided is minimal, so specific new findings or mechanisms cannot be detailed from this text alone.
papers.why: Calcium signaling is a critical upstream regulator of autophagy and mitophagy in neurons, making this relevant to understanding calcium-dependent control of mitophagy in interneurons.

papers.title: Mitophagy–pyroptosis–macrophage polarization crosstalk in cardiovascular diseases: mechanistic insights and therapeutic potential
papers.summary: This paper reviews how mitophagy (selective clearance of damaged mitochondria), pyroptosis (an inflammatory form of cell death), and macrophage polarization interact with each other in cardiovascular disease. It discusses the molecular mechanisms linking these three processes and how their crosstalk contributes to disease progression. The paper also explores potential therapeutic strategies that target this crosstalk to treat cardiovascular conditions.
papers.why: While centered on cardiovascular disease rather than the brain, this paper's mechanistic focus on mitophagy pathways and their crosstalk with inflammatory cell death could offer transferable insights into mitochondrial quality control mechanisms relevant to neuronal mitophagy research.

papers.title: PINK1-dependent Mitophagy Mediates CD8+ T Cell Residency and Drives Psoriatic Relapse via CCR4-CCL17/22 Recruitment
papers.summary: This study investigates how PINK1-dependent mitophagy, a process that clears damaged mitochondria, helps CD8+ T cells stay resident in the skin during psoriasis. The researchers show that this mitophagy pathway supports T cell survival and function in tissue, and that recruitment via CCR4 and its ligands CCL17/22 contributes to relapse of psoriatic skin lesions. The findings link mitochondrial quality control in immune cells to chronic inflammatory disease recurrence.
papers.why: While focused on immune cells rather than neurons, this paper offers mechanistic insight into PINK1-dependent mitophagy pathways that may be conceptually relevant to understanding mitophagy regulation more broadly, including in neuronal contexts.

papers.title: Exploring the impact of nutrition and autophagy on infectious diseases to inform the development of homeostatic-nanomedicines for HIV-TB coinfections.
papers.summary: This paper looks at how nutrition status and autophagy pathways influence the course of infections, using HIV-TB coinfection as a key example. It argues that malnutrition or altered nutrient sensing can impair autophagy, weakening the body's ability to control these pathogens. The authors propose using this biology to design 'homeostatic-nanomedicines' that restore autophagic balance as a therapeutic strategy against HIV-TB coinfections.
papers.why: Since autophagy is a core mechanism in this PhD project, understanding its regulation by nutrition in infectious disease contexts could offer transferable insights into autophagy/mitophagy modulation strategies relevant to neuronal health and disease.
